1:
The heading promises a prophecy that does not arrive, and each voice accounts for it differently. John Gill reports two Jewish commentators who refer it forward to a message delivered ten days later, and a third who takes it as a general title to everything from here to the end of the book; Gill prefers the third. Matthew Henry calls the title misapplied and refers it to the later message, the intervening story being an introduction that shows its occasion. Charles Ellicott agrees with Gill, that the words head the whole section of prophecies collected after the capture of the city. John Calvin puts it as a habit of the writer: the chapter begins as though the introduction were forgotten, and we must wait until the narrative is finished before the prophecy is resumed.

How the prophet came to be in chains at all divides them further. Henry supposes he was honourably released from the prison and afterwards, being found among the people when orders went out to bind everyone of consequence, was through ignorance bound with the rest and hurried away; he breaks off to call him a man born to hardship, a man of sorrows indeed. John Wesley agrees, that he was carried off by mistake and against the orders of the king, and that the captain, calling over his prisoners, found him among them contrary to expectation; Gill has him discovered at the muster to the captain’s great surprise. Calvin will have none of it. On his reading the general had Jeremiah brought there still in chains and released in the sight of everyone, not to degrade him but as an indirect reproof to the people, honouring the servant of God who had warned them for more than forty years; the chains were kept on so that the wickedness of the nation might be publicly exposed. Adam Clarke is occupied with the grammar of the opening clause, where Blayney, on the order of the sentence and the commoner use of the verb, refers the words to his being brought before the general for his discharge rather than carried there captive. Ellicott identifies the town as one in Benjamin about six miles from the capital, used as a depot where prisoners waited for orders about their disposal; the chains, he notes, were manacles fastened at the wrists.

The speech of the captain is the third division. Henry makes much of it: the man owns the prophet as true and glories in having been the instrument to fulfil what Jeremiah had been the messenger to foretell, which was on that account the most glorious action he ever did; and what the princes of Israel would never acknowledge from the pulpit they are told from the bench by a conqueror they dare not contradict, since sooner or later men are made sensible that their sin is the cause of their miseries. Calvin goes further, saying the general undertook the prophetic office, God raising up such a teacher because the people had rejected celestial truth for forty years: if we reject the prophets sent to us, other teachers will arise who will deride us and, ungodly themselves, upbraid us with our impiety. Ellicott sets a limit to this. It is significant, he grants, that the general speaks as if recognising the God of Israel and the mission of the prophet, but such recognition implied no more than the ordinary belief that each nation had its guardian deity; the respect shown to Jeremiah he ascribes to the policy he had advocated and perhaps to the influence of Daniel and his friends. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the wording of the speech is that of Jeremiah, though the general may well have expressed the thought, and gloss the promise about the eye as a taking under protection. Clarke reduces the offer to a sentence, that the prophet was now at full liberty.
5:
The fifth verse opens obscurely, and John Gill says the versions have made it hard to tell whose words they are and of whom they are spoken, one Jewish commentator taking them for the words of God. John Wesley reads the scene plainly: the prophet, before leaving the general’s presence, showed himself more inclined to stay, and was told to go back. Charles Ellicott supposes a change of mind in the general, who seems to have felt on second thoughts, perhaps after an answer the narrative does not record, that he had not taken enough precaution for the prophet’s safety, and consigned him again to the care of his friend. The parting gifts, he notes, are those given to an honoured guest, food from the general’s own table and money in compensation for what the prophet had suffered as a preacher of submission. Adam Clarke puts the advice in a sentence: if he means to stay, he had best put himself under his countryman’s protection.

Ellicott finds the official title significant. Gedaliah is made governor over the cities of Judah, not the capital, which is treated as though blotted out and needing no superintendence. He had evidently acted on the counsel of the prophet and accepted the conqueror’s sovereignty as for the time the ordinance of God, and a true patriot might well hold it his duty in such a season to take office under an enemy, in the hope of doing something for the remnant left in his charge. John Calvin reads the whole permission providentially. The king, he says, was convinced of the honesty of Jeremiah, knowing that a man of his standing could have raised great disturbances had he not been quiet; but the deeper reason was that the prophet should give proof of his religion. Had he gone to Chaldea the confidence of many would have failed, since his going might have been read as a sign of hopeless despair; and so God inclined the minds of the conquerors to let him remain, as though to raise a standard for the captives and secure their return after seventy years. Calvin allows that he was afterwards carried into Egypt and died there, but says this in no way frustrated the prophecies, since violent men took him and he did not go willingly.

On the refusal Calvin dwells on the risk the prophet ran. Chaldea was a pleasant and fertile country, and tyrants cannot bear to have their bounty despised, a refusal being taken as a dishonour to themselves; the prophet might easily have been overcome by modesty or fear. That he dared to decline, and asked instead to live in his own country, Calvin takes as evidence that he cared more for religion and the church of God than for any favour of men or wealth of Babylon. Gill sees it from the other side, allowing it might have gone better with him at Babylon, but that he chose to suffer affliction with the people of God rather than live at ease in a foreign and idolatrous country. Keil and Delitzsch supply the background of what follows, that during the conquest many of the men of war had dispersed through the land and fled.

The site of Mizpah is disputed, and Ellicott sets out the case. The name means watch-tower and was not uncommon, six or seven towns bearing it; this is the Mizpah of Benjamin, prominent in the history of Samuel and Saul. One scholar identified it with a village about six miles north of the capital, while three others place it on the ridge continuing the Mount of Olives northward, which Josephus calls by a Greek word meaning watch-tower, apparently rendering the old Hebrew name; the second identification, Ellicott adds, suits the narrative better. Gill puts it briefly, a city in Benjamin about five miles from Jerusalem on the same authority.
7:
Charles Ellicott marks a new section beginning here and running to the murder of Gedaliah. The commanders who had fought the invader in open country found it hopeless to continue after the capital fell, and the king of Babylon, by appointing a prince of Judah, had shown a disposition to treat the conquered leniently; they could do no better than apply to him. Where these men had been is disputed. John Gill offers two possibilities and prefers the second. they either lurked in the fields during the siege, not daring to attack the besieging army, or fled with the king when the city was taken and dispersed about the country. John Calvin rejects that: it does not seem probable that any escaped, since all the companions of the king were overtaken together in the plain; he thinks rather that these were men who abandoned the cities committed to them at the first approach of the enemy, and notes that the word rendered forces means only that they had once been set over towns. John Wesley keeps both options open, supposing them commanders of small parties little regarded by an enemy intent on taking the capital.

Matthew Henry treats the passage as a break in the weather, a bright sky opening on the remnant after years of terror; the prophet, he notes, had nowhere foretold such good days immediately after the captivity, though Providence seemed to raise the expectation, and to a miserable people it would be as life from the dead. The choice of governor he takes as policy: to keep them easy the king commissioned not one of his own princes but one of their brethren, a man of wisdom and mild temper under whom the few left might have been happy. The conqueror was so well satisfied as to feel no jealousy at the numbers gathering; and it would be a great reviving for the dispersed to come together again under a governor of their own nation, so that in wrath God remembered mercy. Calvin adds that God bestowed no common honour on Gedaliah, who while seeking nothing was set over the land, and that though his power was short the divine will was to give a pious man some evidence of favour. Gill explains the return simply: the besieging army was gone and a governor of their own nation in place, much preferable to captivity abroad.

The list of names sets the grammarians working. Keil and Delitzsch identify Ishmael as a grandson of Elishama and of royal blood, note that one of the sons of Kareah is omitted in the parallel passage, place the home of the sons of Ephai near Bethlehem, and derive the last captain from a district in Syria near Hermon, his name being spelt differently in the parallel list. Ellicott agrees that Ishmael was of the seed royal, though there is no means of fixing his place in the line of succession, and reports that two of the captains are named in the parallel passage and nothing more is known of them; he places the town of the sons of Ephai in Benjamin, and takes the last captain for a naturalised alien from a small kingdom east of the Jordan. Keil and Delitzsch add the motive: these men had borne arms against the Chaldeans and were concerned for their safety on returning. Both Calvin and Adam Clarke look ahead. Clarke identifies Ishmael as the man who afterwards murdered the governor, employed for it by the king of the Ammonites, with whom he seems to have sheltered during the siege; Calvin says envy moved him to kill a man who had received him kindly, a reward for the deed coming from the same quarter. The sons of Kareah pledged their faith to the governor, Calvin adds, but he was too credulous and closed his ears to wise counsel and warning.
9:
The oath needs explaining first. John Gill supplies the fear behind it: these men had encouraged the king to hold out the siege, and might expect to be demanded and given up once it was known where they were, so the governor not only promised safety but swore to it. John Calvin agrees that an oath was not strange in so disturbed a time, and that in quiet times it would not have been needed; their life hung as it were on a thread. He also finds a risk in the reception itself: it did not please the conquerors that such men should remain in the land, the princes having been killed and the chief men carried off lest any attempt new commotions, the object being to keep the country quiet. Gedaliah must have seen that what he did would not be welcome, and his humanity prevailed. Charles Ellicott states the undertaking in official terms: acting as satrap, he assures them that although they had fought against the conquerors there would be a full amnesty, he remaining at his post and they returning to their homes.

On the tenth verse Gill notes that the governor urges his own example, the town he fixed on being a frontier place on the road to Babylon, a fit residence for a deputy; the phrase about serving he glosses as standing before the messengers who came for tribute or with orders, all of which he would take on himself, acting besides as advocate for his people. John Wesley adds only that the place was convenient for receiving orders. Calvin makes the promise weightier: in undertaking to stand before the Chaldeans for them the governor laid down his own life, becoming surety that nothing grievous should happen, which shows he did not regard himself but used his power for the public good. Instead, Calvin says, he spread his wings like a hen to gather the remnant of his nation under them. On the clause about the cities Calvin prefers the plainest sense of an ambiguous verb, since a handful of men could not have taken a city by force: they might safely remain wherever they were. Ellicott dates the scene from the produce: the fruits show it was autumn, and the captains were invited to help themselves from fields and vineyards whose owners had been carried off, to relieve immediate want and provide for the winter.

The return of the scattered is the brief high point of the chapter. Wesley traces the dispersion in stages, many fleeing at the first invasion and more as the conquest went on, until word came that a governor of their own religion and country was set over the land; the country being nearly empty and wonderfully fruitful, they gathered plenty of grapes and other summer fruits. Gill sees a flourishing commonwealth in prospect, princes and soldiers and common people gathered in large numbers under one government. Calvin reads the passage as showing that but for wickedness at home their condition would have been endurable until the seventy years had run, God so moderating his vengeance that a remnant remained until the restoration. The governor did not deceive them, he insists, since the exiles dwelt in safety and God gave them abundance, so that men who had been wanderers in great poverty now lived comfortably at home. From that he draws the indictment the chapter is moving towards: their ingratitude is the more detestable because they were not moved by the destruction of the city, the burning of the temple and the slaughter, nor by hearing the captain of the guard preach the vengeance of God and perform the office of a prophet in reproving them; having despised the kindness shown them, they rushed on their own ruin by killing their governor, an act that might have provoked the conqueror to blot out the very name of the people.
13:
John Calvin opens the last section: the wrath of God had not been appeased by the destruction of the city and the temple. The appointment of a governor was a token of mercy; but now he is killed, a scattering follows, and the anger of the conqueror is kindled besides, the guards left with him being killed too. The assassin, he says, had been hired and advised by the king of the Ammonites; and Calvin guesses at the motive, that the king may have hoped to hold the land himself once the invading army withdrew, and, finding that hope disappointed, turned to making the country desolate. John Gill observes that the informant seems to have been the chief captain after Ishmael, who is absent because the charge is against him; John Wesley notes that these men had been with the governor before, but come now to disclose a conspiracy.

The refusal to believe them divides the commentators sharply. Adam Clarke makes it a proof of greatness. The whole account of the man, he says, shows uncommon greatness of soul: conscious of his own integrity, he took the portrait of others from his own mind, and believed evil of no one because he felt none in his own breast. He may be reproached as too credulous, but whatever is charged against him on that head only shows the greatness of his mind, since a little soul is ever suspicious and ready to believe the worst of every person and thing, while a great mind acts always on the contrary. Calvin will not have it. He calls the man blinded, so that he not only disregarded the counsel but rejected the help offered; he allows it was praiseworthy not to have Ishmael killed out of hand while the cause was unknown. But there is a medium, he insists, between simplicity and cruelty. He ought to have inquired, and having found the matter out could have defended himself and punished a public pest, holding authority as no private man; instead he wilfully closed his eyes and committed a great mistake. He wronged the informers too, who were not one or two men but the chiefs set over the soldiers, so that their charge was probable.

Behind this lies a harder question, which Calvin puts directly: how was it that God allowed a holy man of such rare virtues to be basely killed by an assassin? His first answer is that the judgments of God are just though they do not answer to our notions, and that it was the divine purpose both to take this man to himself and to execute vengeance on a people wholly unworthy of favour. His second is that when God calls his servants out of this world he regards their good, so that death itself is a mercy: had the governor lived longer he would have met things more bitter than a hundred deaths, and would have watched the people struggle against the goodness of God until their ruin came. His third is that virtue and fault were mixed in one act: love is not suspicious and ought not easily to admit an accusation, yet he should have been more cautious, not for his own sake only but because his death brought the ruin of the whole people. Clarke, having praised the man, concedes the cost in a sentence: had he been a little more distrustful he would have saved his own life, and so a noble man lost it by not believing of others an evil of which he was himself incapable. Gill notes the manner of the two approaches: the question was put not because they supposed he knew already but so that he might be assured the thing was matter of fact, and the second warning was given secretly, to prevail with him more easily and because the proposal was not fit for the public.
